message.content:
The number of mitochondria in a cell is highly variable and depends largely on the cell’s metabolic demands. In general:

| Cell type (or tissue) | Typical range of mitochondria per cell |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Red blood cells** (which lack mitochondria) | 0 |
| **Neurons** (high energy demand) | ~1 000–5 000 |
| **Cardiac muscle cells** (continuous contraction) | ~5 000–10 000 |
| **Skeletal muscle cells** (intense bursts of activity) | ~10 000–20 000 |
| **Liver hepatocytes** (metabolic hub) | ~500–2 000 |
| **Epithelial cells** (moderate demand) | ~200–1 000 |
| **Stem cells** (low metabolic rate) | ~50–200 |

These numbers are approximate averages; individual cells can vary by a factor of two or more. The key point is that cells with high ATP requirements—such as muscle fibers, neurons, and cardiac myocytes—harbor thousands of mitochondria, whereas cells with lower energy needs may contain only a few hundred or none at all (e.g., mature red blood cells).
